author: Ben Horowitz
description: Horowitz, a venture capitalist and former chief executive, writes about the hardest parts of building and running a company, drawing on his experience leading a struggling technology business. He discusses layoffs, firing executives, managing through crises, building culture and the psychological strain on leaders. Founders and managers facing difficult decisions will find candid advice grounded in real situations.

title: The Hidden Life of Trees
author: Peter Wohlleben
description: Wohlleben, a German forester, describes how trees in a forest interact, drawing on scientific research and his own observations. He explains how trees may share nutrients through root and fungal networks, respond to threats and support their offspring. Written in an approachable, sometimes personal style, it suits nature lovers and general readers curious about forest ecology.

title: The History of the Ancient World
author: Susan Wise Bauer
description: Bauer surveys the ancient world from the earliest written records through the fall of Rome, moving between Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, China, Greece and other regions. She focuses on rulers, wars and the stories societies told about themselves, presented in short chronological chapters. It suits general readers and homeschool families wanting a readable narrative overview of ancient history.

title: The Hobbit
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
description: Bilbo Baggins, a comfort-loving hobbit, is recruited by the wizard Gandalf to join thirteen dwarves on a quest to reclaim their treasure from the dragon Smaug. The journey takes him through encounters with trolls, goblins, elves and giant spiders, and he gains courage along the way. Tolkien's fantasy adventure suits younger readers and adults alike.

title: The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book
author: Andriy Burkov
description: Burkov condenses the core ideas of machine learning into a short book, covering supervised and unsupervised learning, key algorithms, neural networks, model evaluation and practical issues such as feature engineering. Explanations use mathematical notation but stay brief. It suits practitioners wanting a quick refresher and students seeking a compact map of the field before moving to deeper texts.

title: The Hunger Games
author: Suzanne Collins
description: In the nation of Panem, a ruling Capitol forces each district to send two young people to fight to the death in a televised contest. Sixteen-year-old Katniss Everdeen volunteers to take her younger sister's place. Collins's dystopian novel explores survival, inequality and media spectacle, and suits teens and adults who enjoy fast-paced speculative fiction.

title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
author: Rebecca Skloot
description: Skloot tells the story of Henrietta Lacks, a Black woman whose cancer cells were taken without her knowledge in 1951 and became the first human cell line to grow indefinitely in a laboratory. She traces the cells' role in medical research alongside the experiences of the Lacks family. The book raises questions about consent, race and ethics in science.

title: The Index Card
author: Helaine Olen
description: Olen and Pollack argue that sound personal finance advice is simple enough to fit on an index card. They expand on a short list of rules, such as saving a meaningful share of income, paying off credit cards, using low-cost index funds and being wary of financial salespeople. The book suits readers wanting straightforward guidance without complex strategies.

title: The Innovator's Dilemma
author: Clayton M. Christensen
description: Christensen examines why well-managed, successful companies often lose their leading positions when new technologies emerge. He distinguishes sustaining innovations from disruptive ones that start in small or low-end markets and later overtake incumbents, using industries such as disk drives as case studies. Managers, strategists and business students will find an influential framework for thinking about technological change.

title: The Innovators
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Isaacson traces the history of the digital revolution, from Ada Lovelace's ideas about computing machines through the invention of the computer, transistor, microchip, personal computer, internet and web. He emphasises that innovation usually came from collaboration among teams rather than lone geniuses. Readers interested in technology history and the people behind it will find an engaging group portrait.

title: The Intelligent Investor
author: Benjamin Graham
description: Graham sets out the philosophy of value investing, stressing the difference between investing and speculation, the importance of a margin of safety and the need to control emotions during market swings. He contrasts defensive and enterprising investors and explains how to analyse securities. Later editions add commentary relating his ideas to modern markets, making it useful for long-term investors.

title: The Kite Runner
author: Khaled Hosseini
description: Amir, a boy from a wealthy family in Kabul, betrays his loyal friend Hassan, a servant's son, and carries the guilt into adulthood after fleeing to the United States. Years later he returns to a Taliban-ruled Afghanistan seeking redemption. Hosseini's novel explores friendship, fathers and sons, and a country's upheavals, and suits readers of contemporary literary fiction.

title: The Lean Mindset
author: Mary Poppendieck
description: Mary and Tom Poppendieck apply lean thinking to software and product development, emphasising purpose, customer focus, energised teams and learning through experimentation. Drawing on examples from various organisations, they discuss how teams can deliver value quickly while staying aligned with real needs. Product managers, engineering leaders and agile practitioners will find ideas for building effective, motivated teams.

title: The Lean Product Playbook
author: Dan Olsen
description: Olsen offers a step-by-step process for building products customers want, organised around achieving product-market fit. Stages include identifying target customers and their unmet needs, defining a value proposition, specifying a minimum viable product, prototyping and testing with users. Product managers, founders and designers will find concrete frameworks and examples for reducing risk when developing new products.

title: The Lean Startup
author: Eric Ries
description: Ries proposes a scientific approach to building new ventures under conditions of uncertainty. Central ideas include the build-measure-learn loop, minimum viable products, validated learning, actionable metrics and deciding when to pivot or persevere. Founders, product teams and managers launching new initiatives inside larger organisations will find a practical method for testing ideas before investing heavily.

title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
author: John C. Bogle
description: Bogle, founder of Vanguard, makes the case for buying and holding a low-cost fund that tracks the whole stock market. He explains how fees, trading costs and taxes erode returns for active investors, and why most fund managers fail to beat the market over time. Concise and data-driven, it suits new and experienced investors seeking a simple long-term strategy.

title: The Lord of the Rings
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
description: Frodo Baggins inherits a powerful ring created by the Dark Lord Sauron and sets out with a fellowship of companions to destroy it before it can be reclaimed. Tolkien's epic follows their journey across Middle-earth through war, friendship and sacrifice. With its invented languages, histories and detailed world-building, it suits readers who enjoy immersive high fantasy.

title: The Lucifer Effect
author: Philip Zimbardo
description: Zimbardo examines how ordinary people come to commit cruel acts, drawing heavily on his 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment, which he recounts in detail. He links its lessons to the abuses at Abu Ghraib prison and argues that situations and systems shape behaviour more than is often assumed. The final chapters turn to resisting harmful social pressure and to everyday heroism, making it useful for students of social psychology and ethics.

title: The Martian
author: Andy Weir
description: Stranded alone on Mars after his crew leaves him for dead during a dust storm, astronaut Mark Watney must find ways to survive with limited food, air and equipment. The story alternates his wry log entries with efforts on Earth and aboard his crew's ship to bring him home. Readers who enjoy problem-solving, real science and dry humour will find it an engaging survival thriller.

title: The Master Algorithm
author: Pedro Domingos
description: Domingos surveys the main schools of machine learning, which he calls the five tribes: symbolists, connectionists, evolutionaries, Bayesians and analogizers. He explains each approach's core ideas without heavy mathematics and makes the case for a single universal learning algorithm that could combine them. It suits general readers, students and professionals wanting a conceptual map of how computers learn from data.

title: The Millionaire Next Door
author: Thomas J. Stanley
description: Based on surveys and interviews with wealthy Americans, Stanley and Danko find that many millionaires live modestly, spend below their means and build wealth steadily over decades. The authors contrast these savers with high earners who display success through consumption but accumulate little. Readers interested in personal finance and the habits behind long-term wealth will find practical lessons here.

title: The Miracle Morning
author: Hal Elrod
description: Elrod proposes a structured early-morning routine as a way to improve health, focus and personal growth. His approach combines six practices: silence, affirmations, visualization, exercise, reading and scribing, or journaling. The book draws on his own recovery from a serious car accident and suits readers looking for a simple framework for building daily habits.

title: The Mom Test
author: Rob Fitzpatrick
description: Fitzpatrick offers a practical guide to talking with potential customers without being misled by polite but useless feedback. He shows how to ask about people's real past behaviour and problems rather than pitching an idea and seeking approval. Short and direct, it is aimed at founders, product managers and anyone validating a business idea through customer conversations.

title: The Mythical Man-Month
author: Frederick P. Brooks Jr.
description: Drawing on his experience managing IBM's System/360 and OS/360 projects, Brooks examines why large software projects run late and over budget. His essays cover the problems of adding staff to late projects, the value of conceptual integrity and the absence of any single silver bullet for software productivity. Project managers, engineers and students of software engineering still consult it for its insights into team and schedule dynamics.

title: The Name of the Wind
author: Patrick Rothfuss
description: Kvothe, a legendary figure now living quietly as an innkeeper, begins telling the true story of his life to a travelling chronicler. His account follows a childhood with a troupe of performers, a hard stretch as an orphan on city streets and his entry into a university where magic is studied as a science. Fans of richly detailed epic fantasy with a strong first-person voice will enjoy this first volume of the Kingkiller Chronicle.

title: The Night Circus
author: Erin Morgenstern
description: A mysterious circus that opens only at night becomes the arena for a long contest between two young magicians, Celia and Marco, bound to it by their mentors. As the competition unfolds over years, the pair fall in love and the stakes grow for everyone connected to the circus. Notable for its atmospheric, visual writing and nonlinear structure, the novel suits readers of literary fantasy and romance.

title: The Obstacle Is the Way
author: Ryan Holiday
description: Holiday applies the ideas of Stoic philosophy, especially those of Marcus Aurelius, to modern setbacks and difficulties. He organizes the book around three disciplines, perception, action and will, and illustrates them with stories of historical figures who turned adversity into advantage. It suits readers looking for an accessible introduction to Stoicism and a practical way of handling problems at work and in life.

title: The Omnivore's Dilemma
author: Michael Pollan
description: Pollan traces four food chains from source to plate: industrial agriculture built on corn, large-scale organic farming, a small pasture-based farm, and a meal he hunts and gathers himself. Along the way he examines the ecological, economic and ethical consequences of how Americans eat. Readers curious about where their food comes from and the choices behind it will find it informative and thought-provoking.

title: The Order of Time
author: Carlo Rovelli
description: Rovelli, a theoretical physicist, explores what modern physics says about the nature of time. He explains how relativity, thermodynamics and quantum gravity undermine everyday ideas of a universal present and a steady flow of time, and considers why we nevertheless experience time as passing. Written in short, lyrical chapters with little mathematics, it suits curious general readers interested in physics and philosophy.

title: The Paradox of Choice
author: Barry Schwartz
description: Schwartz argues that an abundance of options, often seen as a sign of freedom, can leave people anxious, indecisive and less satisfied. Drawing on psychological research, he distinguishes maximizers, who seek the best possible option, from satisficers, who settle for good enough. He closes with practical suggestions for reducing the burden of decisions, making it useful for readers interested in consumer behaviour and wellbeing.

title: The Personal MBA
author: Josh Kaufman
description: Kaufman condenses the core ideas of business education into a broad set of concise mental models for self-directed learners. Topics range across value creation, marketing, sales, finance, systems and human psychology, each explained briefly with practical examples. Aspiring entrepreneurs, managers and anyone weighing the cost of a formal MBA can use it as an accessible overview and reference.

title: The Phoenix Project
author: Gene Kim
description: Told as a novel, the story follows Bill, an IT manager suddenly put in charge of rescuing a failing, overdue project at a struggling manufacturing company. With guidance from a mentor, he learns to apply lean manufacturing ideas such as flow, feedback and continual learning to IT operations. Written by Kim with co-authors, it introduces DevOps principles in an accessible way for engineers, managers and business leaders.

title: The Power of Habit
author: Charles Duhigg
description: Duhigg explains the science of how habits form and how they can be changed, centred on a loop of cue, routine and reward. He applies this framework to individuals, companies and social movements, using case studies from sports, business and medicine. Readers who want to understand their own behaviour or lead change in organizations will find practical ideas grounded in research.

title: The Power of Now
author: Eckhart Tolle
description: Tolle presents a spiritual teaching centred on living fully in the present moment rather than being ruled by thoughts about the past and future. Drawing on elements of Buddhism, Christianity and other traditions, he describes how identification with the mind creates suffering and how awareness can loosen it. Written largely in question-and-answer form, it suits readers interested in mindfulness and spiritual growth.

title: The Power of Positive Thinking
author: Norman Vincent Peale
description: Peale, a Protestant minister, combines Christian faith with practical advice on building confidence, overcoming worry and pursuing goals with optimism. Each chapter offers techniques such as prayer, affirmations and visualization, illustrated with stories from people he counselled. It suits readers looking for an inspirational, faith-based approach to self-improvement and gives insight into a long-influential strand of American self-help.

title: The Pragmatic Programmer
author: Andrew Hunt
description: Hunt and Thomas offer a collection of practical tips on the craft of software development, from writing flexible code to managing a career. Ideas such as not repeating yourself, orthogonality, tracer bullets and automation are explained in short, focused sections that can be read independently. Programmers of any experience level who want to improve their habits and professional judgment will find it a lasting reference.

title: The Pragmatic Programmer: 20th Anniversary Edition
author: David Thomas
description: Thomas and Hunt revise their guide to software craftsmanship for a new generation of developers, updating examples and adding material on topics such as concurrency, security and modern development practices. The core advice remains, covering code design, testing, debugging, estimation and taking responsibility for one's work. It suits both newcomers and experienced programmers who want practical guidance on writing maintainable software and developing their careers.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
description: Housel argues that success with money depends more on behaviour than on technical knowledge. Through short, story-driven chapters, he explores ideas such as the power of compounding, the role of luck and risk, the value of saving without a specific goal and the meaning of having enough. Readers at any stage of their financial lives will find a thoughtful look at how emotions and personal history shape money decisions.

title: The Psychology of Selling
author: Brian Tracy
description: Tracy focuses on the mental side of sales, arguing that a salesperson's self-concept and attitude strongly affect results. Alongside this, he offers practical techniques for prospecting, presenting, handling objections and closing. Aimed at sales professionals and anyone whose work involves persuasion, it combines motivational advice with step-by-step methods for improving performance.

title: The Richest Man in Babylon
author: George S. Clason
description: Set in ancient Babylon, a series of parables follows characters who learn simple rules for building and protecting wealth. Lessons include saving a portion of all earnings, controlling spending, avoiding risky schemes and putting money to work through sound investment. Originally issued as separate pamphlets, the stories offer an easy introduction to personal finance principles for readers of any age.

title: The Righteous Mind
author: Jonathan Haidt
description: Haidt, a social psychologist, examines why people divide so strongly over politics and religion. He argues that moral judgments arise mainly from intuition, with reasoning following afterwards, and uses moral foundations theory to explain how liberals and conservatives prioritize different values. Readers interested in moral psychology, political polarization and understanding opposing viewpoints will find it a clear, research-based account.

title: The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich
author: William L. Shirer
description: Shirer, an American journalist who reported from Berlin in the 1930s, traces Nazi Germany from Hitler's rise to the regime's defeat in 1945. The narrative combines his own observations with captured German documents, diaries and records presented at the Nuremberg trials. Detailed and comprehensive, it suits readers seeking a thorough single-volume history of the Third Reich and the Second World War in Europe.

title: The Road
author: Cormac McCarthy
description: A father and his young son travel on foot across a burned, ash-covered America in the years after an unexplained catastrophe. Pushing a shopping cart of supplies toward the coast, they face cold, hunger and the threat of other survivors who have turned to violence. McCarthy writes in sparse prose about love, survival and moral endurance, suiting readers of literary fiction prepared for a bleak setting.

title: The Selfish Gene
author: Richard Dawkins
description: Dawkins presents evolution from the perspective of the gene, arguing that organisms can be understood as vehicles built by genes to ensure their own replication. He uses this view to explain behaviours such as altruism, cooperation and family conflict, drawing on game theory and the work of other evolutionary biologists. The book also introduces the meme as a unit of cultural transmission and suits readers interested in biology and evolution.

title: The Shining
author: Stephen King
description: Jack Torrance, a recovering alcoholic and struggling writer, takes a winter caretaker job at the isolated Overlook Hotel in the Colorado mountains, bringing his wife Wendy and young son Danny. Danny has psychic abilities, and the hotel's dark history begins to work on the family as snow cuts them off from the world. King's novel combines supernatural horror with a study of addiction and family breakdown.

title: The Silent Patient
author: Alex Michaelides
description: Alicia Berenson, a painter, shoots her husband and then stops speaking entirely, refusing to explain what happened. Years later, psychotherapist Theo Faber takes a job at the secure unit where she is held, determined to get her to talk and uncover the truth. This psychological thriller suits readers who enjoy unreliable narrators, mental health themes and plots built around a central mystery.

title: The Silk Roads
author: Peter Frankopan
description: Frankopan retells world history by placing the regions linking Europe and Asia, from the Middle East to Central Asia, at the centre rather than the periphery. He follows the movement of goods, religions, ideas, diseases and armies along these routes from antiquity to the present. The broad narrative suits readers who want a fresh perspective on global history beyond a Western-centred account.

title: The Silk Roads: A New History of the World
author: Peter Frankopan
description: Rather than viewing the past from Western Europe, Frankopan shows how the lands between the Mediterranean and China shaped the growth of empires and the exchange of trade and beliefs. Chapters are organized around themes such as faith, slaves, oil and wheat, tracing connections from ancient Persia to modern geopolitics. History readers and students looking for a wide-ranging global account will find it informative.

title: The Simple Path to Wealth
author: JL Collins
description: Collins developed this guide from letters to his daughter about money and investing. He advocates avoiding debt, saving a large share of income and investing in low-cost, broad stock market index funds, then holding through market downturns. Readers who want a straightforward, low-maintenance strategy toward financial independence will find clear explanations without jargon.

title: The Singularity Is Near
author: Ray Kurzweil
description: Kurzweil argues that technological progress is accelerating exponentially and predicts a point, which he calls the Singularity, when machine intelligence will surpass and merge with human intelligence. He discusses advances in genetics, nanotechnology and robotics and considers their implications for health, longevity and society. Readers interested in futurism, artificial intelligence and debates about the long-term direction of technology will find it a key reference.

title: The Sixth Extinction
author: Elizabeth Kolbert
description: Kolbert, a journalist, investigates the idea that Earth is undergoing a mass extinction driven by human activity. Visiting scientists in places such as the Amazon, the Great Barrier Reef and Panama, she examines species loss linked to climate change, ocean acidification, habitat destruction and invasive species. The book combines field reporting with scientific history and suits readers concerned about biodiversity and the environment.

title: The Splendid and the Vile
author: Erik Larson
description: Larson recounts Winston Churchill's first year as British prime minister, from May 1940 through the Blitz. Using diaries, letters and official records, he portrays Churchill alongside his family, advisers and staff as London endured German bombing. Readers of narrative history interested in the Second World War and leadership under pressure will find an intimate, closely observed account.

title: The Startup Owner's Manual
author: Steve Blank
description: Blank and Dorf present a detailed, step-by-step guide to the customer development process for building a startup. The manual explains how to test business model hypotheses by talking directly with customers, then validate the model, create demand and scale. Its workbook-style checklists suit founders, entrepreneurship students and teams launching new products in both web and physical markets.

title: The Story of My Life
author: Helen Keller
description: Keller tells her own story of growing up deaf and blind after an illness in infancy, and of the arrival of her teacher Anne Sullivan. She describes learning language through touch, her schooling and her studies at Radcliffe College. The autobiography offers readers of all ages a firsthand account of determination, learning and the bond between student and teacher.

title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck
author: Mark Manson
description: Manson offers a blunt, humorous take on self-help, arguing that a good life comes from choosing carefully what to care about rather than trying to feel positive all the time. He discusses accepting limits, taking responsibility, embracing uncertainty and valuing meaningful struggles. Readers tired of conventional upbeat advice will find a direct, conversational approach to values and personal priorities.

title: The TCP/IP Guide
author: Charles M. Kozierok
description: Kozierok provides an extensive reference to the TCP/IP protocol suite and the technologies behind the internet. Starting with networking fundamentals and the OSI reference model, it covers addressing, routing, IPv4 and IPv6, TCP and UDP, and application protocols such as DNS, HTTP and email. Network engineers, students and IT professionals can use it both for study and as a detailed reference.

title: The Tangled Web
author: Michal Zalewski
description: Zalewski, a security researcher, explains how modern web browsers work and why their design makes web applications hard to secure. He covers URLs, HTTP, HTML, scripting, the same-origin policy and other browser security mechanisms, highlighting their inconsistencies and pitfalls. Web developers and security professionals will gain a deeper understanding of the browser environment their applications depend on.

title: The Tipping Point
author: Malcolm Gladwell
description: Gladwell explores how ideas, products and behaviours spread through society in ways similar to epidemics. He introduces concepts such as the Law of the Few, the stickiness factor and the power of context, illustrating them with case studies from fashion, crime and public health. Readers interested in social trends, marketing and how small changes can produce large effects will find it accessible.

title: The Total Money Makeover
author: Dave Ramsey
description: Ramsey sets out a step-by-step plan for getting out of debt and building wealth, organized around a sequence he calls the Baby Steps. The programme includes building an emergency fund, paying off debts from smallest to largest with the debt snowball, and later investing for retirement and paying off the home. Readers struggling with debt who want a firm, structured plan will find direct guidance.

title: The Untethered Soul
author: Michael A. Singer
description: Singer explores consciousness and the inner self, encouraging readers to observe their thoughts and emotions rather than identify with them. Drawing on meditation and spiritual traditions, he discusses letting go of fear and past pain and choosing to remain open instead of closing down. It suits readers interested in mindfulness, spirituality and inner peace.

title: The War of Art
author: Steven Pressfield
description: Pressfield identifies an internal force he calls Resistance that keeps writers, artists and others from doing their creative work. In short sections, he describes how it appears as procrastination, fear and self-doubt, and argues for overcoming it by approaching work as a professional rather than an amateur. Creators and anyone struggling to begin or finish ambitious projects will find practical encouragement.

title: The Warmth of Other Suns
author: Isabel Wilkerson
description: Wilkerson chronicles the Great Migration, in which millions of Black Americans left the South for cities in the North and West between roughly 1915 and 1970. She follows three people who made the journey in different decades, weaving their stories together with broader historical research. Readers interested in American history, race and migration will find a deeply researched and personal account.

title: The Web Application Hacker's Handbook
author: Dafydd Stuttard
description: Stuttard and Pinto walk through how attackers probe web applications and turn weaknesses into working exploits. Topics include attacking authentication, session management and access controls, injection flaws, cross-site scripting and logic errors, with a structured methodology for testing. Penetration testers, security students and developers who want to understand attacks in order to build safer applications will find it a thorough reference.

title: The Wright Brothers
author: David McCullough
description: McCullough tells the story of Wilbur and Orville Wright, two bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, who achieved the first powered airplane flight. Drawing on family papers and letters, he follows their experiments at Kitty Hawk, their persistence through failure and their later demonstrations in Europe and America. Readers interested in aviation, invention and American history will find a well-researched biography.

title: Think and Grow Rich
author: Napoleon Hill
description: Hill presents principles for achieving success and wealth, which he says he drew from studying prominent figures of his era. Chapters cover ideas such as desire, faith, autosuggestion, persistence and the mastermind group. Considered a foundational text of the self-help genre, it suits readers interested in motivation, goal-setting and the history of success literature.

title: Thinking in Bets
author: Annie Duke
description: Duke, a former professional poker player, applies lessons from poker to making decisions under uncertainty. She warns against judging decisions only by their outcomes and encourages thinking in probabilities, acknowledging luck and seeking honest feedback from others. Professionals, investors and anyone making choices without complete information will find practical tools for improving judgment.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
description: Kahneman describes two modes of thinking: a fast, intuitive System 1 and a slower, deliberate System 2. Drawing on decades of research, much of it with Amos Tversky, he explains biases such as anchoring, loss aversion and overconfidence, along with prospect theory. Readers interested in psychology, economics and why people make predictable errors in judgment will find a detailed, research-based guide.

title: To Kill a Mockingbird
author: Harper Lee
description: In a small Alabama town during the Depression, young Scout Finch watches her father Atticus, a lawyer, defend a Black man wrongly accused of raping a white woman. Told through Scout's eyes, the novel follows her and her brother Jem as they confront racism, injustice and the mystery of their reclusive neighbour Boo Radley. It suits readers of all ages and is widely studied in schools.

title: Unbroken
author: Laura Hillenbrand
description: Hillenbrand tells the life story of Louis Zamperini, an Olympic runner who became a bomber crewman in the Second World War. After his plane crashed into the Pacific, he survived weeks adrift at sea before being captured and held in Japanese prisoner-of-war camps. The book follows his endurance and his difficult postwar recovery, suiting readers of war history and survival stories.

title: Venture Deals
author: Brad Feld
description: Feld and Mendelson explain how venture capital financing works, from the people involved to the terms that appear in a term sheet. They cover valuation, liquidation preferences, control provisions, convertible notes and negotiation tactics in plain language. Founders raising money, aspiring investors and lawyers new to startups will find a practical reference for understanding deals.

title: When Breath Becomes Air
author: Paul Kalanithi
description: Kalanithi, a neurosurgeon in training, wrote this memoir after being diagnosed with stage IV lung cancer in his mid-thirties. He reflects on his path from literature to medicine, his work with patients and what makes life meaningful in the face of death. Published after his death with an epilogue by his wife Lucy, it suits readers interested in medicine, mortality and memoir.

title: Where the Crawdads Sing
author: Delia Owens
description: Abandoned by her family as a child, Kya Clark grows up alone in the marshes of coastal North Carolina, where townspeople dismiss her as the Marsh Girl. When a well-known local young man is found dead, suspicion falls on her. Blending a coming-of-age story, nature writing and a courtroom mystery, the novel suits readers who enjoy atmospheric fiction.

title: You Are a Badass
author: Jen Sincero
description: Sincero offers an informal, humorous guide to overcoming self-doubt and changing habits that hold people back. Short chapters mix personal anecdotes with advice on self-acceptance, mindset, money and taking action toward goals. Readers who prefer a casual, irreverent voice in self-help will find it an approachable starting point.

title: You Don't Know JS: Scope & Closures
author: Kyle Simpson
description: Simpson explains how JavaScript handles scope, covering lexical scope, function and block scope, hoisting and how the engine looks up variables. Building on these foundations, he gives a clear account of closures and how they underpin patterns such as modules. Developers who use JavaScript but want to understand how the language actually works will find it a focused, in-depth guide.

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel
description: Thiel, a co-founder of PayPal, argues that real progress comes from creating new things rather than copying what already works. Based on a course he taught at Stanford, the book discusses monopoly versus competition, the importance of secrets, the power law in venture investing and building durable companies. Entrepreneurs and readers interested in startups and innovation will find a contrarian view of business strategy.
